concepts.title: Aggregate Built-ins: sum, min and max

questions.q: Using the method 'Aggregate Built-ins: sum, min and max', work with: the fixed constants of the method. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of subtotal.
questions.a: 284 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Aggregate Built-ins: sum, min and max' and work with: the fixed constants of the method. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of subtotal.
questions.a: 284 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Aggregate Built-ins: sum, min and max' refers to.
questions.a: Three ready-made functions read a numeric list in one call: sum() totals the elements, min() returns the smallest and max() the largest, without disturbing the list itself.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Aggregate Built-ins: sum, min and max'.
questions.a: For the list [34, 12, 63, 39, 92, 44] the three calls answer 284, 12 and 92.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Aggregate Built-ins: sum, min and max', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: total = sum(list1)

questions.q: Using the method 'Average Marks with a Function', work with: m1 = 50, m2 = 100, m3 = 10, m4 = 300, m5 = 80, students = 40. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of average.
questions.a: 13.5 years

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Average Marks with a Function' and work with: m1 = 15, m2 = 25, m3 = 150, m4 = 80, m5 = 8, students = 300. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of average.
questions.a: 0.9267 years

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Average Marks with a Function' refers to.
questions.a: The function computeAverage(list1, n) walks the collected marks, folds each into a running total, and divides by the number of students to produce the class average.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Average Marks with a Function'.
questions.a: The list is built with append() inside an input loop before the averaging function ever runs.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Average Marks with a Function', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: average = total_marks / students

questions.q: Using the method 'Append versus Extend', work with: added_count = 100, base_len = 300. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of after_extend.
questions.a: 401 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Append versus Extend' and work with: added_count = 60, base_len = 4. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of after_extend.
questions.a: 65 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Append versus Extend' refers to.
questions.a: append() drops its whole argument in as one single new element, even when the argument is itself a list, while extend() unwraps the argument list and attaches each element separately, so the two calls grow a list by different amounts.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Append versus Extend'.
questions.a: Appending [50, 60] adds one nested element; extending with [80, 90] adds two flat elements.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Append versus Extend', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: after_extend = after_append + added_count

questions.q: Using the method 'Negative Step Slicing of Lists', work with: size = 4096, step_size = 4096. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of kept.
questions.a: 1 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Negative Step Slicing of Lists' and work with: size = 512, step_size = 2048. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of kept.
questions.a: 1 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Negative Step Slicing of Lists' refers to.
questions.a: Slicing works on lists exactly as on strings: list1[n:m] copies positions n up to m minus 1, and a negative step walks from the end backwards, so list1[::-1] hands back the whole list reversed and list1[::-2] keeps every second element from the right.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Negative Step Slicing of Lists'.
questions.a: A first index larger than the second yields an empty list, and a runaway second index shrinks to the list end.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Negative Step Slicing of Lists', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: kept = (abs(span) + step_size - 1) // step_size

questions.q: Using the method 'Linear Search Position', work with: zero_based_index = 25. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of position.
questions.a: 26 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Linear Search Position' and work with: zero_based_index = 500. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of position.
questions.a: 501 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Linear Search Position' refers to.
questions.a: The function linearSearch(num, list1) compares the target with each element from the front; on a match it returns the zero-based index, which the caller converts to a human-friendly position by adding one, and it returns None when nothing matches.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Linear Search Position'.
questions.a: A target at index i costs i comparisons on elements before it, and the i plus oneth comparison finds it.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Linear Search Position', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: position = zero_based_index + 1

questions.q: Using the method 'Nested List Student Record', work with: the fixed constants of the method. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of percent.
questions.a: 78.8 per cent

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Nested List Student Record' and work with: the fixed constants of the method. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of percent.
questions.a: 78.8 per cent

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Nested List Student Record' refers to.
questions.a: A record such as ['Raman', 'A-36', [56, 98, 99, 72, 69], 78.8] nests the five subject marks inside a list, so two indices reach a single mark as stRecord[2][j], and dividing the inner total by five rebuilds the stored percentage.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Nested List Student Record'.
questions.a: The first index picks the inner list, the second picks the element inside it.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Nested List Student Record', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: percent = (m1 + m2 + m3 + m4 + m5) / 5

concepts.title: Alias versus Clone of a List

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Alias versus Clone of a List' refers to.
questions.a: Assigning list2 = list1 only binds a second name to the same list object, so changes through either name show up in both; a genuine independent copy needs slicing with [:], the list() constructor, or copy.copy().

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Alias versus Clone of a List'.
questions.a: After appending 10 through list1, the alias list2 also shows 10, while a clone still holds the old contents.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Alias versus Clone of a List', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: clone = old_list[:] or list(old_list) or copy.copy(old_list)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Insert, Remove and Pop Shifting' refers to.
questions.a: Because a list is mutable and ordered, insert() pushes later elements one place right, remove() deletes only the first match of a value, and pop() extracts the element at a given index (or the last one) while shrinking the list.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Insert, Remove and Pop Shifting'.
questions.a: Every insertion or deletion shifts the positions of the elements after the affected index.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Insert, Remove and Pop Shifting', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: new_len = old_len - 1 after one pop or remove
